meta.title: Who really said "Hasta la victoria siempre"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine: Che Guevara closed his farewell letter to Fidel Castro with “Hasta la victoria siempre.” Castro read it aloud in Havana on 3 October 1965.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Hasta la victoria siempre'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Che Guevara: the last line of his farewell letter to Fidel Castro, read aloud by Castro in Havana on 3 October 1965. The only dispute is over a comma.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is the last line of Guevara’s farewell letter to Fidel Castro, written in Spanish. Castro read the letter aloud in Havana on 3 October 1965, and the official transcript of that speech ↗ ends the letter with “Hasta la victoria siempre. ¡Patria o Muerte!”

source.heading: The farewell letter to Fidel Castro

docMeta.dd: Carta de despedida a Fidel Castro (farewell letter)
Undated, headed “Habana, Año de la Agricultura”. Castro said it was handed to him on 1 April 1965
Read aloud by Fidel Castro at the Teatro Chaplin, Havana, 3 October 1965. Reprinted in Obra revolucionaria (Era, México, 1967)
Original in Spanish. Common English renderings include “Until victory, always” and “Ever onward to victory!” There is no single authorized translation

source.excerpt:
Tendría muchas cosas que decirte a ti y a nuestro pueblo, pero siento que son innecesarias, las palabras no pueden expresar lo que yo quisiera, y no vale la pena emborronar cuartillas.

Hasta la victoria siempre.
¡Patria o Muerte!
Te abraza con todo fervor revolucionario,
Che.
trail: Castro introduced the letter as “una carta aquí de puño y letra, transcripta a máquina, del compañero Ernesto Guevara”. He said it carried no date and had been handed to him on 1 April 1965. His reading ends “Hasta la victoria siempre. ¡Patria o Muerte!” (speech transcript ↗)

The UNAM journal Chiapas (no. 5, 1997) reprints the letter from Guevara’s Obra revolucionaria (Era, 1967), with the note “Leída por Fidel Castro el 3 de octubre de 1965”. It closes with the same line (Chiapas reprint, PDF ↗)

Wikiquote lists Hasta la victoria siempre in its sourced section for the “Farewell letter to Fidel Castro (1965)”, glossed as “Until victory always” (Wikiquote: Che Guevara ↗). Quote Investigator has no article on the phrase (QI search ↗)
Aleida March, Guevara’s widow, writes in her memoir that he regretted putting the comma in the wrong place. Biographer Jon Lee Anderson disagrees (El Observador / BBC Mundo, 2019 ↗)
source.excerptNote: Closing lines of the letter as Castro read it on 3 October 1965, from the official speech transcript. In English: “I would have many things to say to you and to our people, but I feel they are unnecessary; words cannot express what I would like them to, and there is no point in scribbling pages. Until victory, always. Homeland or death! I embrace you with all my revolutionary fervor, Che.” Some transcriptions punctuate the line differently (see below).

source.rightsNote: The line comes from Guevara’s farewell letter. Castro made it public on 3 October 1965, and it was reprinted in Obra revolucionaria (Era, 1967). Under US rules a work first published in 1931 or later is presumed still in copyright, so treat the letter as in copyright. A four-word slogan quoted on its own is a different matter from reproducing the full letter.

author.name: Che Guevara
author.heading: About Che Guevara
author.metaLine: 1928–1967 · Argentine-born Marxist revolutionary, a leader of the Cuban Revolution
author.bio: Ernesto Guevara was a physician from Argentina who became one of the leaders of the Cuban Revolution alongside Fidel Castro. After the revolution he held senior posts in Cuba’s government. In 1965 he gave up those posts to fight elsewhere, and he was killed in Bolivia on 9 October 1967. His farewell letter to Castro is the source of the slogan ¡Hasta la victoria siempre!

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong about it
misattribution.intro: Che Guevara attracts a lot of invented quotes, but this one is genuinely his. The confusion is about how the line is punctuated, how it is dated, and a famous song with a similar title.

items.who: “Hasta la victoria, siempre Patria o Muerte”
items.why: Aleida March says in her memoir Evocación that Guevara regretted misplacing the comma. On her account he meant “until victory, [it is] always Homeland or Death”, not “until victory, always”. Jon Lee Anderson does not believe there was any error (El Observador / BBC Mundo ↗). Wikisource prints the comma version (Wikisource ↗). Castro’s transcript prints “Hasta la victoria siempre.” as its own line.
Many English sources date the letter “April 1, 1965” (marxists.org ↗). Castro said the letter was deliberately left undated and that 1 April was the day he received it (speech transcript ↗).
Puebla’s 1965 song is a reply to the farewell letter, and its title borrows part of Guevara’s saying. The lyric is not Guevara’s own line (Wikipedia ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Guevara’s own: they close his farewell letter to Fidel Castro, which Castro read aloud in Havana on 3 October 1965 (official transcript ↗).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: By late 1965 Guevara had not been seen in public for months, and rumors in the foreign press said he had been purged or was ill. On 3 October 1965 Castro presented the first Central Committee of the newly renamed Communist Party of Cuba. Guevara was absent from it, and Castro explained why by reading his letter aloud. In the letter Guevara resigned his party post, his ministry, his rank of comandante and his Cuban citizenship, so that he could fight “against imperialism wherever it may be” (transcript ↗).
The letter’s last line became a slogan of the Cuban Revolution and of the left more widely (Wikipedia ↗). It was given wider reach the same year by Carlos Puebla’s song “Hasta siempre, comandante”.
detailsBody: Transcriptions of the letter differ. Castro’s official speech transcript and the Obra revolucionaria reprint both set “Hasta la victoria siempre.” apart as its own line, followed by “¡Patria o Muerte!”. Wikisource gives “Hasta la victoria, siempre Patria o Muerte”. According to the BBC Mundo report, the handwritten original breaks the line after “Hasta la victoria”, and Aleida March reads the comma as a slip (El Observador ↗). Either way the words are Guevara’s. Only how they divide is in question.
